blocks: A best response is the move that does best for you against one specific move by the other player.
So it is always a question about one column or one row at a time: which of your moves pays most if they play this?
steps.callout: Best response is about one specific move by the other player. A dominant strategy is best against every move.

annotations.text: If the column player picks Left, Top pays the row player 2 and Bottom pays 1. So Top is the best response to Left.
If the column player picks Right, Bottom pays 3 and Top pays 0. So Bottom is the best response to Right.

hints: Take one column at a time. In that column, which row gives the row player the larger number?
Top against Left is already underlined. Underline the row player's other best response.

blocks: A Nash equilibrium is a cell where each player is already at a best response to the other's move.
It is stable in one sense: no one gains by switching alone. It is not a claim that this is the best outcome, or what people will pick.
steps.callout: Stable means no one gains by switching alone. It does not mean best for everyone.

annotations.text: Top and Left: each is a best response to the other, so neither gains by switching alone.
Bottom and Right is also stable. A game can have more than one equilibrium.

hints: A cell is an equilibrium when the row player's number is the largest in its column and the column player's number is the largest in its row.
Check each of the four cells. Two of them pass both checks.

blocks: An outcome is Pareto efficient when no other outcome makes one player better off and no one worse off.
Pareto efficiency is about the outcome alone. It says nothing about whether the outcome is stable.
steps.callout: Stable (Nash) and efficient (Pareto) are different tests. An outcome can pass one and fail the other.

annotations.text: Defect and Defect is stable: neither player gains by switching alone.
Cooperate and Cooperate pays both players more. Defect and Defect is not Pareto efficient, because this cell is better for both.

hints: Find the stable cells first. Those are the equilibria, and they may not be efficient.
Defect and Defect is the only stable cell here.

blocks: A strategy is strictly dominant when it pays more than each alternative against every move the other player could make.
Dominance is about your own options. It does not say the result is good for anyone.
steps.callout: Dominant means best against every move. Best response means best against one move.

annotations.text: Against Cooperate, Defect pays the row player 5, and Cooperate pays 3. Against Defect, Defect pays 1 and Cooperate pays 0.
Defect is better in both columns, so Cooperate is strictly dominated. It can be removed from the row player's options.

hints: Compare the two rows column by column. Is one strategy better in every column?
Cooperate is worse for the row player in both columns, so it can go.

blocks: Iterated elimination removes a strictly dominated strategy, then looks again at the smaller game.
A strategy that was not dominated before can become dominated once another one is gone.
steps.callout: Remove one dominated strategy at a time, then check the smaller game again.

annotations.text: Push pays the row player more in both columns, so Hold is strictly dominated and goes first.
With Hold gone, the column player only has Left and Right against Push. Left pays 1 and Right pays 0, so Right goes next.

hints: Look for a row that is better than another in every column.
Hold is beaten by Push in both columns.

blocks: In a Prisoner's Dilemma, each player is better off defecting whatever the other does, yet both do better when both cooperate.
The payoffs are what the players care about. If a player cares about the other's outcome, the payoffs change, and so does the game.
steps.callout: Defecting is dominant, and mutual defection is still stable but not Pareto efficient.

annotations.text: Defect and Defect is the only stable cell. Neither player gains by switching alone.
Cooperate and Cooperate pays both more. The game is a dilemma because the stable cell is not the efficient one.

hints: For each cell, ask whether either player would gain by switching alone.
Only one cell has no profitable switch.

blocks: In a Stag Hunt, both players do best by matching each other, and there are two stable matches.
One match pays both players more. The other is safer, because it does not depend on the other player joining in.
steps.callout: Stag Hunt has two stable cells, and one of them pays more to both. Prisoner's Dilemma has one.

annotations.text: Stag and Stag is stable, and it pays both players the most.
Hare and Hare is also stable. It pays less, but it does not need the other player to join in.

hints: A stable cell has each player at a best response to the other.
Two cells pass the test. Find both.

blocks: In Chicken, each player does best by going straight when the other swerves, and swerving when the other goes straight.
If both go straight, both get the worst payoff, so the stable outcomes are the two where one swerves.
steps.callout: In Chicken, mutual straight is the worst outcome, and there is no dominant strategy.

annotations.text: Swerve against Straight: the row player swerves, and the column player goes straight. Neither gains by switching alone.
The mirror cell, Straight against Swerve, is stable too.

hints: Straight and Straight is the worst cell for both. Is it stable?
Check the two cells where one player swerves and the other goes straight.

blocks: In a pure coordination game, both players get the same payoff whenever they match, and nothing when they do not.
There are two stable matches. The problem is choosing which one to aim for, not which one pays more.
steps.callout: In pure coordination, the players agree on what matters. Only the matching counts.

annotations.text: Option A and Option A pay both players 1, and neither gains by switching alone.
Option B and Option B is also stable, and pays the same. Only the matching matters.

hints: Look at the matching cells first.
Both matching cells pass the test.

blocks: In Battle of the Sexes, both players prefer to match, but they disagree about which match.
Each stable match favours one player, so the game is a coordination problem with a conflict in it.
steps.callout: Battle of the Sexes has two stable matches, and the players disagree about which one they prefer.

annotations.text: Opera and Opera is stable. The row player gets 2 there, and the column player gets 1.
Football and Football is also stable, and the payoffs flip in favour of the column player.

hints: Both matching cells are stable here, and the mismatched cells are not.
Find both matching cells.
